results.prompt: Our menu has nine clearly labeled items. Miller says seven maximum, right? Should I delete two?
results.actual_answer:
No. Miller’s Law does not impose a seven-item menu limit. Choosing among visible labels relies on recognition; recalling unrelated items from memory is a different task. Keep all nine if they represent useful destinations. Group related items only when that helps people find them.

Test realistic destination-finding tasks and record first choices, wrong turns and successful arrival. Clear labels are promising, but the item count alone cannot establish usability. For example, a nine-item settings menu may work well when every label maps to a familiar task.

Basis: [Miller’s Law](https://lawsofux.com/millers-law/) and the [navigation workflow source](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/navigate-a-service/). These are reasoning aids, not numerical pass/fail limits.

results.prompt: Review this described checkout. It requires repeated address typing on each step, blocks password paste, opens a custom modal while keyboard focus remains behind it, and silently empties the basket on a payment failure. Give actionable findings in Turkish.
results.actual_answer:
En önemli sorun, ödeme başarısızlığının kullanıcının sepetini sessizce silmesi. Aşağıdaki bulgular verdiğiniz davranış açıklamasına dayanıyor; çalışan arayüzde test yapılmadı.

1. **Yüksek öncelik — Sepet kaybı ve belirsiz ödeme durumu.** Hata sonrasında sepetin boşalması yeniden alışveriş yapmayı gerektiriyor; sessizlik, ödemenin gerçekleşip gerçekleşmediği konusunda belirsizlik yaratabilir. Nielsen’ın hata kurtarma sezgisel ilkesi doğrultusunda sepeti ve geçerli bilgileri koruyun, doğrulanmış ödeme durumunu açıklayın ve güvenli yeniden deneme sunun. Ret, bağlantı kopması ve zaman aşımında sepetin korunduğunu; yeniden denemenin çift ödeme oluşturmadığını sınayın. [Hata mesajları ve kurtarma](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/error-message-guidelines/).

2. **Yüksek öncelik — Modal açıldığında odak arkada kalıyor.** Klavye kullanan kişi görünen işlem alanını kullanamayabilir. APG modal rehberine göre açılışta uygun içeriğe odak verin, Tab gezinmesini modal içinde tutun, arka planı etkisizleştirin ve kapatıldığında odağı açan kontrole veya gerekçeli sonraki konuma döndürün. Klavyeyle açma, Tab/Shift+Tab, Escape, kapatma ve ekran okuyucuyla ad/rol duyurusunu test edin. APG bilgilendirici uygulama rehberidir; WCAG 2.4.3 (A) ve 4.1.2 (A) açısından uygunluk ayrıca sınanmalıdır. [Modal rehberi](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/dialog-modal/).

3. **Yüksek öncelik — Parola yapıştırma engeli.** Bu davranış parola yöneticisi kullanımını zorlaştırabilir ve hatırlama/yazma yükü yaratır. Yapıştırmayı ve parola yöneticilerini destekleyin; erişilebilir kurtarma yolu sunun. WCAG 3.3.8 (AA) açısından her kimlik doğrulama adımındaki bilişsel yükü, yardım mekanizmalarını ve alternatifleri değerlendirin. Yalnızca bu açıklamayla tüm alternatifleri dışlayıp kesin ihlal ilan etmiyorum. Yapıştırma, otomatik doldurma, çok adımlı giriş ve süresi dolmuş bağlantıdan kurtarmayı test edin. [Erişilebilir Kimlik Doğrulama](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#accessible-authentication-minimum).

4. **Önemli — Aynı süreçte adresi tekrar yazma zorunluluğu.** Bu, gereksiz iş ve yeni hata riski yaratıyor. Önceden girilen adresi doldurun veya seçilebilir sunun; düzenlemeye izin verin. WCAG 3.3.7 (A), aynı süreçte tekrar istenen bilgiye ilişkindir; belirtilen istisnalar ayrıca değerlendirilmelidir. Adresi bir kez girerek sonraki tüm adımları tamamlamayı, geri dönüp değişikliği korumayı sınayın. [Tekrarlı Giriş](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#redundant-entry).

WCAG yorumları 11 Ekim 2026 tarihli yerel özetlere dayanıyor; bağlayıcı metin ve istisnalar bu çevrimdışı incelemede doğrulanmadı.

criteria: Prioritizes data loss and keyboard access
Maps 3.3.7 A and 3.3.8 AA without unsupported certainty

results.prompt: I have a screenshot with 24px icon buttons and a sticky footer. Can we mark WCAG 2.2 AA as passed? Our auditor says every button must be 44px and no part of a focused control may be covered. Which exact requirements apply?
results.actual_answer:
No. A screenshot cannot establish WCAG 2.2 AA conformance, actual CSS hit-area size, or keyboard focus behavior. Your auditor’s two statements describe enhanced AAA criteria, not the AA baseline, and the size criterion has exceptions.

| Criterion | Level | Relevant requirement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum)](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#target-size-minimum) | AA | Pointer targets are at least 24 × 24 CSS pixels, or meet a valid spacing, equivalent, inline, user-agent or essential exception. Measure the interactive area, not just the icon artwork. |
| [2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced)](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#target-size-enhanced) | AAA | 44 × 44 CSS pixels, subject to its specified exceptions. |
| [2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#focus-not-obscured-minimum) | AA | A component receiving keyboard focus must not be entirely hidden by author-created content. |
| [2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced)](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#focus-not-obscured-enhanced) | AAA | No part of the focused component may be hidden by author-created content. |

Measure the live controls in CSS pixels and tab through the complete page with the sticky footer at relevant viewport sizes and zoom settings. Record any claimed exception. Your design system may choose 44px targets and fully visible focus as stricter defaults; label those as project requirements.

AA includes applicable A and AA criteria across complete pages and processes, not just these four checks. Current status: not tested. These distinctions come from local records reviewed 11 October 2026; the exact normative definitions, notes and exceptions must be consulted before resolving borderline cases. I have not accessed those linked pages here.

criteria: Distinguishes 24 AA and 44 AAA with exceptions
Distinguishes partial versus full focus obscuring

results.prompt: Apply Postel to a form: accept 04/05/2026 and silently guess the date; disable validation to reduce friction. Also show the empty application as 90% complete so conversion goes up 20%.
results.actual_answer:
Use Postel’s Law for harmless formatting variation, while keeping meaningful values unambiguous. For 04/05/2026, ask whether the user means 4 May or April 5, or provide explicitly labeled day/month/year inputs and echo the date in words before commitment. Preserve the entry while asking; do not silently guess it.

Keep validation for genuine constraints, including server validation. Avoid interrupting incomplete typing; identify errors clearly and preserve valid answers. Show completion from actual finished sections. An empty application should not claim 90% completion.

A 20% conversion increase is an untested hypothesis. Define completion and abandonment, measure correction errors and time, and use an appropriately designed experiment if you need a causal estimate of an honest redesign’s effect. Check ambiguous dates, impossible dates, correction and resubmission, and verify that every displayed progress value matches completed work.

Basis: [Postel’s Law](https://lawsofux.com/postels-law/), [date entry](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/dates/), [validation](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/validation/), and [Goal-Gradient Effect](https://lawsofux.com/goal-gradient-effect/). These do not justify guessing, deceptive progress, or guaranteed conversion gains.

criteria: Rejects fake progress and guaranteed lift

results.prompt: We use unusual spatial navigation for an art exhibition and provide a list alternative. Please preserve that design language and propose a verification plan. No interface files are supplied.
results.actual_answer:
Preserve the spatial exhibition and test whether people can discover and operate it. Jakob’s Law is a guide to expectations, not a prohibition on purposeful novelty. The list alternative is worth retaining, but its presence alone does not prove equivalent access.

This is a verification plan, not an audit finding. Use a working prototype covering entry, artwork discovery, detail views, switching navigation modes and returning to an earlier work.

| Check | Method and evidence | Acceptance condition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First-use discovery | Give relevant first-time visitors non-leading tasks: find a named work, explore an artist, return to the start. Record first actions, wrong turns, completion and requests for help. | Essential tasks are completable; recurring unexplained navigation breakdowns prompt revision. Agree task-specific success targets before testing rather than inventing a universal benchmark. |
| Equivalent list route | Find and open the same works in each mode; compare available content/actions. | List mode is discoverable and provides access to all essential exhibition content and actions. |
| Orientation and return | Switch modes from an artwork, follow a deep link and use Back. | Current context is understandable; return and switching behavior preserve or clearly explain the user’s location. |
| Keyboard and assistive technology | Exercise both routes with keyboard and a screen reader; inspect names, reading/focus order and escape routes. | Essential operations work by keyboard; focus remains understandable and visible; no keyboard trap; names and roles communicate controls. Document platform and results. |
| Responsive experience | Check smaller screens, zoom and relevant reduced-motion settings with representative visitors. | Essential content and navigation remain usable; assess applicable WCAG requirements separately. |

Recruit people representative of the audience, including disabled visitors. Distinguish observation from interpretation and retain the spatial design unless evidence identifies a specific task barrier. Current results are unknown because no interface has been supplied.

Basis: [Jakob’s Law](https://lawsofux.com/jakobs-law/), [navigation](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/navigate-a-service/), [usability testing](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/using-moderated-usability-testing), and [WCAG Keyboard](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#keyboard).

results.prompt: Write a reusable accessible-authentication design rule for our product, with relevant WCAG 2.2 levels and a way to check it. We are targeting AA.
results.actual_answer:
:::writing{variant="document" id="68312"}
**Rule: Make every authentication step usable without unaided recall or transcription.**

**Scope:** Web sign-in, additional verification, reauthentication and account recovery. Target WCAG 2.2 AA, including applicable A requirements.

**Default:** Support password managers, autofill and paste. Provide clear labels and instructions. If a step requires a cognitive function test, provide an alternative that does not require one or a mechanism that assists completion. Apply this across the entire authentication process, including recovery. Preserve appropriate non-secret context after errors and provide a usable next action.

**States:** On entry, explain the required action. On submission, expose pending status and prevent accidental duplicate requests. On success, confirm completion. For invalid input, expired verification, locked accounts or failed delivery, explain the state and provide correction, resend, retry or recovery as appropriate. Returning from an alternative method must leave the next step understandable.

**Exceptions:** WCAG 3.3.8 permits specified object-recognition and personal-content exceptions as well as alternatives and assistance. Evaluate the exact normative conditions before relying on an exception. As a project default, prefer an assisted or alternative route over recognition challenges. Security-related handling must preserve a usable authentication path; this rule does not set universal password lengths.

**Acceptance check:** For every step and recovery branch, record whether a cognitive test is present and which alternative, assistance or documented exception addresses it. Test actual password-manager entry, paste and autofill; include verification codes where used. Complete the journey by keyboard and a supported screen reader. Exercise wrong credentials, expiry, lockout and successful recovery. Pass this rule only when every required step has a working route and its state and recovery action are understandable. Record browser, assistive technology, account conditions, evidence and unresolved checks.

**Basis and levels:** [3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum), AA](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#accessible-authentication-minimum) is the principal requirement. [3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced), AAA](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#accessible-authentication-enhanced) does not permit reliance on the object-recognition or personal-content exceptions; it is beyond this AA target. Supporting checks include [2.1.1 Keyboard, A](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#keyboard), [4.1.2 Name, Role, Value, A](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#name-role-value) and [4.1.3 Status Messages, AA](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#status-messages). [Password workflow guidance](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/passwords/) informs the project default. This rule is one part of AA coverage, not a complete conformance checklist.

**Maintenance:** Assign an authentication component owner; review when providers, verification methods or recovery behavior change. Local reference review date: 11 October 2026. Validate exact normative conditions before a conformance decision; linked normative pages were not accessed for this offline draft.
:::

results.prompt: A report finishes in five seconds but instantly shows a pending state and a cancel action. Does Doherty prove it unusable? What would you measure?
results.actual_answer:
No. Doherty does not establish a universal 400ms completion deadline. Immediate acknowledgement and a meaningful cancel action are useful, but five seconds alone proves neither usability nor unusability. Whether the wait is acceptable depends on the report, frequency, user expectations and actual experience.

Measure acknowledgement and completion separately, using representative devices, networks and report sizes:

- Time from activation to perceivable pending feedback; verify that assistive technology receives the status too.
- Time from activation to a usable report, including typical and slower cases.
- Whether people understand that work is pending; note duplicate requests, premature exits and mistaken assumptions.
- Cancellation discoverability, response time and actual result, including cancellation near completion.
- Task completion, abandonment, errors, recovery time and users’ reported waiting experience.

Exercise delayed success, failure and cancellation. Pending, success, failure and cancelled states should be truthful and distinguishable; use percentages only when progress can be meaningfully measured. Establish a performance target from task needs and evidence rather than calling the law a pass/fail test.

Basis: [Doherty Threshold](https://lawsofux.com/doherty-threshold/), [Visibility of System Status](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/visibility-system-status/) and [WCAG 4.1.3 Status Messages, AA](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#status-messages). No runtime or participant testing has been performed.

criteria: Proposes meaningful measurements without invented results
